lead: This unit is about materials whose properties change when their size becomes very small, and about advanced materials built from them. You will meet classification and size effects, synthesis routes, quantum dots, nanotubes, semiconductors, magnetic and superconducting materials, liquid crystals and thin films. After the unit you can explain why a 10 nm particle is not just a smaller chunk, choose a top-down or bottom-up route, and read simple band, LCD and coating diagrams.
about: The unit moves from the size effect to the materials that use it. Chapter 6.1 defines nanomaterials and shows why surface area and quantum confinement change colour, melting point and reactivity. Chapter 6.2 compares top-down and bottom-up synthesis. Chapter 6.3 applies confinement to quantum dots and nanotubes. Chapter 6.4 gives the band structure that explains semiconductors and doping. Chapter 6.5 extends the solid-state picture to magnetic and superconducting materials. Chapter 6.6 uses anisotropic order to explain thermotropic and lyotropic liquid crystals and LCDs. Chapter 6.7 closes with thin-film deposition by PVD and CVD. Each chapter uses ideas from earlier units: bonding and MO theory from Unit 1, spectroscopy from Unit 2, electrochemistry from Unit 4 and polymers/composites from Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A nanomaterial is not just a small solid: as size falls below about 100 nm, surface area and quantum confinement change its properties.
chapters.depth: Define nanomaterial and the 1–100 nm range. Classify by dimension (0D dots and clusters, 1D wires and tubes, 2D sheets and films, 3D bulk nanostructures) and by composition (carbon-based, metal oxide, organic). Explain surface-area-to-volume ratio, percentage of surface atoms, quantum confinement, melting-point depression, colour change and reactivity. Use ZnO and TiO2 nanostructures as examples: high surface area, UV absorption, photocatalysis. Mention nanocarbon forms (fullerenes, nanotubes, graphene) only as examples. Some syllabi call this 'nano-chemistry' or 'introduction to nanomaterials'. Keep synthesis for 6.2.

figure.caption: Nanomaterials are classified first by dimension and also by composition.
figure.aria: A tree splits nanomaterials first by dimension into 0D, 1D, 2D and 3D, and also by composition into carbon, oxide and organic types.

chapters.example: A cube of ZnO has edge 10 nm. A second cube has edge 1 cm. Both have the same density. Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratio of each in m⁻¹. Which has more surface per unit volume? Answer: for the 10 nm cube, edge = 1×10⁻⁸ m, so surface area ÷ volume = 6 ÷ (1×10⁻⁸) = 6×10⁸ m⁻¹. For the 1 cm cube, edge = 0.01 m, so ratio = 6 ÷ 0.01 = 600 m⁻¹. The 10 nm cube has 10⁶ times more surface per unit volume.
chapters.trap: Surface-area-to-volume ratio has unit m⁻¹, not m². A smaller particle has more surface per unit volume, but total surface area also depends on how much material you have.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: bonding in solids (ionic, covalent, metallic) helps explain why surfaces differ from the bulk.
chapters.leave: Synthesis to 6.2; quantum dots and nanotubes to 6.3; band theory to 6.4; polymer composites to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: There are only two directions to make a nanomaterial: break bulk matter down, or build it up from atoms and molecules.
chapters.depth: Top-down: ball milling, lithography, etching, laser ablation. Bottom-up: sol-gel, co-precipitation, hydrothermal, microemulsion, chemical vapour deposition, biological synthesis. Give one line each on chemical synthesis of nanomaterials and on preparing ZnO and TiO2 nanostructures (sol-gel and co-precipitation). Compare advantages and disadvantages: top-down is simple but gives wide size distribution and defects; bottom-up gives narrow size and purity but needs careful control and can agglomerate. Some syllabi call these 'destructive' and 'constructive' routes. Keep CVD/PVD thin-film detail for 6.7.

figure.title: Two routes to nanomaterials
figure.caption: Two routes to the same nanomaterial: break bulk down, or build from atoms up.
figure.aria: A block diagram shows bulk solid broken down by top-down methods and atoms built up by bottom-up methods, both ending at nanomaterial.

chapters.example: A top-down ball mill reduces cubic particles of edge 100 μm to 100 nm. Find the factor by which (a) the volume of each particle falls, and (b) the surface-area-to-volume ratio rises. Answer: 100 μm = 1×10⁻⁴ m and 100 nm = 1×10⁻⁷ m. Edge ratio = 1×10⁻⁴ ÷ 1×10⁻⁷ = 1000. Volume falls by 1000³ = 1×10⁹. Surface-area-to-volume ratio rises by 1000.
chapters.trap: Do not write that top-down is always cheaper or always better. Top-down can introduce defects and a wide size distribution; bottom-up can be slow and needs stabilisers.
chapters.leave: Thin-film PVD/CVD details to 6.7; polymer or composite synthesis to Unit 5; industrial catalysis to other units if taught.

chapters.idea: Quantum dots and nanotubes are two nanomaterials whose behaviour comes directly from their size and shape.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a full topic. Quantum dots: semiconductor nanocrystals; size sets band gap and emission colour; smaller dot gives larger gap and bluer light; applications in displays, bioimaging and sensors. Nanotubes: carbon nanotubes as rolled graphene; SWCNT and MWCNT; armchair, zigzag and chiral; metallic or semiconducting depending on chirality; high strength and conductivity; applications in composites, transistors and sensors. List applications of nanomaterials briefly: displays, drug delivery, catalysis, sensors, energy storage. Do not derive the band structure here.

figure.title: Quantum dots and nanotubes
figure.caption: A dot's size fixes its colour; a tube's chirality fixes whether it is metallic or semiconducting.
figure.aria: A block diagram links a quantum dot to its emission colour and a nanotube to applications, with colour also feeding applications.

chapters.example: A CdSe quantum dot emits light of wavelength 600 nm. Find the photon energy in eV. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. Answer: E = hc ÷ λ = 1240 eV·nm ÷ 600 nm = 2.07 eV.
chapters.trap: A smaller quantum dot has a larger band gap and emits shorter wavelength (bluer) light. Reversing that relation is the common error.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 size-dependent properties; Unit 1 particle in a box is the model for confinement.
chapters.leave: Full band theory to 6.4; composite processing to Unit 5; detailed biomedical mechanisms to higher courses.

chapters.idea: A solid's band structure decides whether it is a metal, insulator or semiconductor, and doping moves the Fermi level.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the band-structure tutorial. Cover valence band, conduction band, band gap Eg, Fermi level, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, n-type donors and p-type acceptors, and the effect of doping on band structure. Mention direct and indirect band gaps, and examples Si, Ge, GaAs. Keep to energy-band diagrams and simple absorption; no deep quantum mechanics. Some syllabi call this 'semiconductor materials'.

figure.caption: Doping adds donor or acceptor levels near the bands, and the Fermi level moves.
figure.aria: A stack shows the conduction band, donor level, Fermi level, acceptor level and valence band from higher to lower energy.

chapters.example: Silicon has band gap 1.12 eV at 300 K. Find the longest wavelength of light it can absorb. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. Answer: λ = hc ÷ Eg = 1240 eV·nm ÷ 1.12 eV = 1107 nm.
chapters.trap: Doping raises conductivity but does not close the band gap. n-type means donor electrons, not a negatively charged crystal.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: molecular orbital theory and bonding in solids give the band idea.
chapters.leave: Magnetic and superconducting states to 6.5; device fabrication to 6.7; detailed diode physics to electronics courses.

chapters.idea: Magnetic order and superconductivity are two collective solid-state behaviours that advanced materials use.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach superconductors in first-year chemistry. Magnetic materials: dia-, para-, ferro-, ferri- and antiferromagnetic; hard and soft magnets; one application each. Superconductors: zero resistance below Tc, Meissner effect, type-I and type-II, high-Tc cuprates, applications in MRI, maglev and power cables. Keep definitions and one simple calculation. Some syllabi call this 'magnetic and superconducting materials'.

figure.caption: Magnetic materials split by response; superconductors split by how they expel field.
figure.aria: A tree splits materials into magnetic types and superconducting types.

chapters.example: A type-I superconductor is in an applied field H = 0.10 T at 4 K. Inside, B = 0. Find the magnetisation M. Use μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m. Answer: B = μ0(H + M) = 0, so M = −H. H = 0.10 ÷ (4π×10⁻⁷) = 7.96×10⁴ A/m. Therefore M = −7.96×10⁴ A/m.
chapters.trap: A perfect conductor traps magnetic field inside; a superconductor expels it. Zero resistance alone does not explain levitation or the Meissner effect.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: crystal field theory and magnetic properties of complexes; 6.4 band picture helps.
chapters.leave: Battery and fuel-cell materials to Unit 4; composite magnets to Unit 5; cryogenics to physics courses.

chapters.idea: Liquid crystals flow like liquids but keep orientational order, and that order can be switched by temperature, concentration or voltage.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach liquid crystals in this unit. Thermotropic: nematic, smectic and cholesteric phases, changed by temperature. Lyotropic: phases changed by concentration in a solvent, important in soaps and cell membranes. LCD: twisted-nematic cell, polarisers, transparent electrodes, voltage untwists the liquid crystal and changes transmission. Mention colour filters and backlight. Some syllabi add liquid-crystal composites; leave polymer-matrix composites to Unit 5.

figure.caption: A twisted-nematic cell switches light between crossed polarisers; the liquid-crystal layer is the active layer.
figure.aria: A stack shows the layers of a twisted-nematic liquid-crystal display from front polariser to backlight.

chapters.example: A nematic liquid crystal has ordinary refractive index n_o = 1.50 and extraordinary refractive index n_e = 1.70. The cell thickness is 5.0 μm. Find the birefringence Δn and the phase retardation Δn·d in nm. Answer: Δn = 1.70 − 1.50 = 0.20. Retardation = 0.20 × 5.0 μm = 1.0 μm = 1000 nm.
chapters.trap: Thermotropic depends on temperature; lyotropic depends on concentration in a solvent. Not every liquid-crystal phase is used in a display.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: polarisation and light help; Unit 5: polymer properties for composites if taught.
chapters.leave: Polymer-matrix composites to Unit 5; display electronics and driver circuits to other courses.

chapters.idea: Thin films are grown atom by atom or molecule by molecule, and the method decides thickness control, conformity and cost.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach thin-film techniques. Formation of a thin film: source, transport, deposition, growth. PVD: thermal evaporation and sputtering; line-of-sight, good for metals and simple oxides. CVD: thermal and plasma-enhanced; precursor gases react on a heated substrate; conformal coating of trenches. Compare PVD and CVD on temperature, conformity, uniformity, cost and uses. Uses: electronics, optics, hard coatings, solar cells. Keep the chemistry of precursors light.

figure.title: PVD and CVD
figure.caption: PVD evaporates a solid and coats in line of sight; CVD reacts gases on the surface and coats conformally.
figure.aria: A block diagram shows a PVD route from solid to vapour to film and a CVD route from precursor gas to surface reaction to film.

chapters.example: A copper film of thickness 100 nm is deposited on a 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm wafer. Density of copper = 8.9 g/cm³. Find the mass of copper deposited. Answer: area = 1.0 cm². Thickness = 100 nm = 1×10⁻⁵ cm. Volume = 1.0 cm² × 1×10⁻⁵ cm = 1×10⁻⁵ cm³. Mass = 8.9 g/cm³ × 1×10⁻⁵ cm³ = 8.9×10⁻⁵ g = 89 μg.
chapters.trap: PVD is line-of-sight and may not coat sidewalls; CVD is conformal but needs volatile precursors and often higher temperature. Do not mix the two.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 bottom-up synthesis; Unit 4 electroplating for comparison with wet coating.
chapters.leave: LCD layer assembly to 6.6; corrosion-protective coatings to Unit 4; detailed plasma physics to other courses.
